title: Jonah runs (Jonah 1–2)
hook: told to go east, he sails west, and prays from inside the fish

segments.voice: Yesterday, Micah's courtroom: not rivers of oil, but justice, mercy and hatznea lechet, a careful walk. Your line was walk humbly.

The word of the Lord came to Jonas, son of Amathi: arise, go to Ninive, the great city, and preach in it. Ninive, Nineveh, was a great city of the Assyrians, far to the east, overland. So Jonah gets up. And he goes down to the port of Joppe, on the coast, finds a ship sailing for Tharsis, far off across the sea to the west, pays the fare, and climbs aboard. He was fleeing, the text says, from the face of the Lord. East was the job. He bought a ticket west.
screen: `ARISE, GO TO NINIVE.` → `NINIVE IS EAST.` → `HE BUYS A TICKET WEST.`

segments.voice: One verb keeps repeating. Jonah went down to Joppe. He went down into the ship. He went down into the inner part of the ship and fell fast asleep. Down, down, down. Then a great storm. The sailors are terrified; each cries to his own god, and they throw the cargo overboard. The captain finds the runaway prophet asleep in the hold: get up, call upon thy God. They cast lots to find whose fault this is, and the lot falls on Jonah. He tells them the truth: I'm a Hebrew, I fear the God who made the sea and the dry land, and I'm running from him. Throw me in, he says, and the sea will calm. And the sailors don't want to. They row hard for land first. Only when they can't make it do they throw him in, and the sea goes quiet, and those sailors end up fearing the Lord and making vows. Then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now the Lord prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonas: and Jonas was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights." The Hebrew says dag gadol, a great fish; there's no whale in the book of Jonah. From inside it Jonah prays, the first time he's prayed in the story. He went down, he says, to the roots of the mountains, and God brought his life up from corruption. Jesus pointed to this story as a sign: Jonah three days in the fish, the Son of man three days in the heart of the earth.
screen: `WENT DOWN, DOWN, DOWN.` · `THE SAILORS ROW FOR LAND FIRST.` · `A GREAT FISH, NOT A WHALE.` · `HE PRAYS FROM THE BOTTOM.` · then, large: `THREE DAYS AND THREE NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Maybe you have a Nineveh too: a conversation you've avoided for months, an apology, a call to a parent, a decision you keep sleeping through like Jonah in the hold. Name it quietly, without scolding yourself, the way Jonah finally told the sailors the truth. If you pray, pray from wherever you are, even if it feels like the bottom.
Jonah runs. The prophet sent east to Nineveh who sails west instead, goes down and down, and finally prays from inside a great fish. Today's word.
Your line: you can't outrun him. Even at the bottom, a prayer. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Jonah at Mass, especially in Lent, and the Church reads Jonah's three days in the fish as a sign of Christ's three days in the tomb, as Jesus does in the Gospels.

fork.setup: you're the ship's captain in a killing storm. the sailors are praying to every god they know, and one passenger is asleep in the hold. what do you do?
options: let him sleep; one less person panicking.
wake him and tell him to call upon his God.
fork.reveal: the captain wakes Jonah: get up, call upon thy God. the pagan sailors pray before the prophet does.

original.note: Hebrew: a great fish. the book never says whale.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man swallowed by a whale.
what it means: a prophet running from God goes down and down, until from the very bottom he finally prays.
what a scholar hears: the verb yarad, went down, repeats as he flees: to Joppe, into the ship, into the hold, to the roots of the mountains.
guess: a prophet fleeing the job God gave him
a prophet chased out of Nineveh by a king
a sailor thrown overboard for stealing

chat.says: Why did Jonah end up inside a fish?
options: He ran west from God's call east; God sent a great fish, and he prayed.
He fell overboard by accident while fishing in a storm near Joppe.
The sailors threw him in to punish him, refusing to row for land.
chat.meaning: Jonah fled the job, going down and down. The Lord prepared a great fish, and from inside it Jonah finally prayed.

Ninive.meaning: the Douay's spelling of Nineveh, a great Assyrian city

Joppe.meaning: the port on the coast where Jonah found a ship

Tharsis.meaning: a far-off place, west across the sea

Assyrians.meaning: the people whose great city was Nineveh

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): removed an anachronism (Nineveh as Assyria's capital after it 'flattened the northern kingdom'; Jonah is set under Jeroboam II, before both); fixed a garbled line ('Only when they can't do they throw him in'); practice no longer says 'everybody has a Nineveh'; softened 'has long read'.
Douay-Rheims wording of Jonas 2:1 (English 1:17) quoted from memory; please check. Douay numbering of Jonah 2 differs from English Bibles by one verse.
Tharsis (Tarshish) is often located in Spain (Tartessos); 'about as far west as a ship from there could go' hedges this. Confirm.
The verb 'went down' (yarad) in 1:3 (twice), 1:5 and 2:6: confirm the count and verses in Hebrew.
Matthew 12:40 in the Douay reads 'whale's belly' (from the Greek ketos); the script says only that the book of Jonah has no whale. Confirm the framing is fair.
Jonah's pre-flight message ('preach in it') follows the Douay's 'preach in it, for the wickedness thereof is come up before me' in paraphrase.
